strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-explored question—how memory addition and deletion policies affect long-term LLM agent behavior—and the empirical scope is commendable: three heterogeneous agents (code generation, autonomous driving, IoT intrusion detection) with different I/O formats and retrieval mechanisms, plus validation across multiple backbones (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3).

The identified phenomena are clearly framed and operationally defined: the experience-following property, error propagation, and misaligned experience replay are each supported by targeted analyses (input/output similarity correlations, error-free memory comparisons in Section 4.4 and Appendix C.2, deleted-vs-retained record analysis in Section 5.3).

The experimental design includes sensible controls, e.g., the error-free variant that replaces retrieved demonstrations with ground truth to isolate error propagation, noisy-initialization ablations, task distribution shift simulation, and memory-capacity-constrained experiments.

Reproducibility artifacts are reasonably thorough: released code/data, detailed appendix with per-agent hyperparameters (deletion periods, thresholds, similarity definitions), and full evaluator prompts.

The practical takeaways (selective addition, history-based deletion when the evaluator is reliable, combined deletion for memory reduction with minimal degradation) are actionable for practitioners designing agent memory systems.
weaknesses: Dependence on an oracle evaluator: the headline results (and the '10% average gain') rest on 'strict' addition/deletion, which checks generated outputs against ground truth at test time. This assumes a level of supervision that largely undercuts the motivation for memory-based self-improvement. The practically deployable 'coarse' LLM evaluator performs much worse (e.g., 31.35 vs. 38.86 on EHRAgent) and history/combined deletion with a coarse evaluator often degrades performance (e.g., 53.08 vs. 60.67 on CIC-IoT), so the paper's central recommendation is only valid under conditions most real deployments cannot meet. The paper acknowledges this but treats fine-tuning as a hand-wavy fix without evidence.

The claimed experience-following property is supported primarily by plots of cumulative average input similarity vs. cumulative average output similarity (Figures 3, 9, 15). Cumulative averages over a shared execution sequence are highly autocorrelated, which can inflate apparent correlations and makes the reported r values difficult to interpret; non-cumulative, per-task analyses (or partial-correlation controls) are needed to establish the property rigorously.

No statistical rigor: results appear to be single runs with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests, despite using stochastic LLM backbones and noticeable variance in the trend plots. Differences of a few points (e.g., Period 39.04 vs. No-del 38.89; Combined 63.50 vs. No-del 63.33 on CIC-IoT) are interpreted as meaningful without uncertainty quantification.

Hyperparameters for deletion strategies (period, α, retrieval-count threshold n, utility threshold β) are reported but their selection procedure is never described, raising concerns of tuning on test data and undermining generality claims; no sensitivity analysis is provided for these thresholds.

Novelty of the core observation is modest: that in-context demonstrations with similar inputs induce similar outputs is largely a known property of in-context learning, and 'select good examples, prune bad ones' is a natural strategy; the contribution is primarily empirical consolidation rather than a new insight or technique. Parallel work (e.g., EM-based memory optimization, structural memory studies) is discussed but not empirically compared against.

Internal inconsistencies and presentation issues: Section 6.2 text says 'As shown in Figure 6' but describes Figure 7; Figures 11 and 12 are captioned 'Addition results' while illustrating deletion/misaligned replay analysis; the code-release footnote is incomplete (empty URL); typos such as 'quality insurance'; some figures (heatmaps in Figure 5, near-saturated axes in Figure 9 for CIC-IoT) are hard to read.

Generality limits: all experiments use one backbone family per setting with small sampled test sets (1200–2392 tasks), the CIC-IoT agent is self-constructed rather than an established framework, and AgentDriver's retrieval is simplified from its original two-step design, so fidelity to the original systems—and hence the claim of studying 'widely adopted' memory designs—is only partial.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-explored question: how memory addition and deletion policies affect the long-term behavior of LLM agents with episodic memory, and it organizes the investigation around a clear research framing.

The empirical study is relatively systematic: it covers three agent settings (EHRAgent, AgentDriver, CIC-IoT), multiple memory addition/deletion strategies, multiple LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3), and two challenging conditions (task distribution shift, memory resource constraints).
The error-free (ground-truth demonstration) control experiments in Sections 4.4 and Appendix C.2 are a thoughtful experimental design that helps isolate error propagation from other effects.
The paper is largely well-motivated and clearly written, with hyperparameters, prompts, and agent designs documented in the appendix, and code/data released, supporting reproducibility.
The misaligned experience replay analysis (Section 5.3), though exploratory, offers a plausible mechanistic explanation for why history-based deletion improves performance.
weaknesses: The strongest results rely on the 'strict' evaluator, which is effectively an oracle that compares agent outputs to ground truth before admitting experiences into memory. Using ground truth at test time to filter memory is a form of label leakage into deployment, so the headline ~10% gain over the baselines has limited practical significance; the deployable 'coarse' LLM-judge variant often underperforms or even degrades with history-based deletion (Table 2), which weakens the practical guidance the paper claims to offer.

The central observations are fairly intuitive and partially anticipated by existing literature: noisy or bad in-context demonstrations degrade performance and selective curation helps are well-known ICL findings; the paper's novelty is mainly in naming ('experience-following', 'error propagation', 'misaligned experience replay') and re-contextualizing these in agent memory, rather than in a new method or a deeper analysis.

Statistical rigor is limited: results appear to be from single runs with no confidence intervals, random seeds, or variance reporting, despite noisy performance trends; several conclusions (e.g., strict addition surpassing the error-free variant around 2000 executions in Figure 4) rest on small differences in noisy curves.

The misaligned experience replay analysis is correlational and post-hoc: the paper hypothesizes that history-based deletion helps by removing 'misaligned' records, but does not directly verify this causal chain (e.g., by re-inserting deleted records or matching on confounders); the heatmaps in Figure 5 are loosely analyzed.

The CIC-IoT agent appears to be a custom, relatively simple prompt-based classifier built by the authors on top of the CIC-IoT dataset rather than an established agent, which weakens the 'three diverse agents' claim; also, retrieval and evaluator setups are simplified from the original AgentDriver pipeline, complicating comparisons to prior work.

Presentation issues and inconsistencies reduce polish: Section 6.2 cites 'Figure 6' but refers to Figure 7; Figures 11 and 12 are captioned 'Addition results for misaligned memory reply' though they concern deletion; a dangling 'ultimately' in Section 5.3; 'Evalution' typo in Figure 1; the CIC-IoT setup paragraph ends without a period.

Some findings are stated more strongly than the evidence supports: e.g., claims of 'general' principles for generic LLM agents drawn from three fairly specific domains, with the no-code, non-tool-using chat-agent space (where much memory research lives) not represented.

strengths: The paper conducts a systematic, well-controlled empirical study of a genuinely under-explored topic: how memory addition and deletion policies shape long-term behavior of LLM agents, evaluated across three diverse agents (code generation for EHR, autonomous driving, IoT intrusion detection) with different input/output formats and retrieval mechanisms.

The identified phenomena—the experience-following property, error propagation, and misaligned experience replay—are clearly defined and supported by quantitative evidence, including a clever 'error-free' experimental design that replaces stored executions with ground truth to isolate the effect of erroneous memory entries.

The proposed mitigation (selective addition plus history-based/combined deletion) is simple, grounded in the analysis (misaligned replay explains the benefit of history-based deletion), and evaluated with ablations: multiple LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3), task distribution shift via GMM clustering, memory resource constraints, and noisy memory initialization.
Hyperparameters, evaluator prompts, similarity computations, and agent designs are documented in detail (Appendix A), and code is released, supporting reasonable reproducibility.
The paper is well organized and honest about limitations of the coarse (LLM-based) evaluator, e.g., that noisy evaluators can propagate errors into deletion decisions.
weaknesses: The headline 'strict' addition and history-based deletion results rely on an oracle evaluator that compares agent outputs against ground truth. This is not deployable in practice and arguably trivializes the problem (filtering by correctness will obviously help). The practically relevant coarse (LLM-judge) strategy shows much smaller or unstable gains, and the paper does not adequately analyze how to close this gap beyond a brief suggestion to fine-tune the evaluator.

No statistical rigor: results appear to come from single runs with no variance estimates, seeds, or significance testing, despite substantial stochasticity from LLM backbones and retrieval; the claimed 'average 10% absolute gain' is driven largely by the oracle condition and is uneven across agents (CIC-IoT gains are marginal).

The central finding—memory-based agents copy similar retrieved demonstrations, so bad demonstrations cause errors—is somewhat intuitive and closely echoes known in-context learning brittleness; the paper's novelty rests mainly on packaging and quantification, and there is no comparison against existing memory management systems (e.g., MemoryBank, AWM, EM-based optimization) as baselines.

'Output similarity' is defined inconsistently across agents (code plagiarism score, RBF against ground truth, embedding similarity), and for AgentDriver it is computed against the ground-truth trajectory rather than between agent outputs, which weakens the generality of the experience-following claim.

Task distribution shift and resource constraint sections are largely descriptive; conclusions are qualitative and the distribution-shift results show small or ambiguous gaps, limiting the strength of the claims there.
Main experiments use only GPT-4o-mini, with the broader backbone check limited to AgentDriver.

strengths: Highly relevant and timely question: how Bearer [REDACTED] addition/deletion operations shape long-term LLM agent behavior, a topic that existing memory-agent papers largely treat as a design detail rather than study directly.

Well-designed experimental matrix: a synthetic, fully controllable RegAgent (where error can be directly measured) combined with three heterogeneous real agents (EHR code generation, autonomous driving, IoT traffic classification) strengthens the generality of the findings.

The error-free (ground-truth replay) variants in Sec 3.4 and B.3 provide a clean causal probe distinguishing error propagation from other effects, and the surprising result that history-based deletion with a strict evaluator can outperform its error-free variant is a genuinely interesting observation.

Consistency checks across multiple LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1-mini, DeepSeek-V3) and across addition/deletion/challenging scenarios (distribution shift, memory capacity constraints) support robustness of the qualitative conclusions.
Extensive appendix (prompts, hyperparameters, evaluator designs, additional plots) and released code/data substantially support reproducibility.

Clear writing with a well-motivated framing (addition and deletion as the two foundational memory operations), and the identified phenomena (experience-following, error propagation, misaligned experience replay) are crisply defined and easy to follow.
weaknesses: The headline recommendation—that a 'strict' evaluator yields the best memory—relies on an oracle-style evaluator (exact-match / ground-truth error thresholds), which is unavailable in many realistic agent settings; the practical gap between strict and achievable automatic evaluators is not closed by the paper's coarse evaluators, limiting the actionable impact of the findings.

The 'experience-following' property is characterized via correlations between cumulative-average input and output similarities; cumulative averaging can inflate Pearson correlations and mask variance, and the paper offers no controlled experiment (e.g., manipulating retrieval similarity with fixed quality) to establish the property causally. The phenomenon also overlaps heavily with known in-context imitation/copying behavior, so novelty is moderate.

The 'misaligned experience replay' explanation is partially circular: misalignment is diagnosed via error-to-ground-truth (the same signal used for strict addition and deletion), so the claim that deletion removes 'misaligned' rather than simply 'erroneous' records is not fully disentangled; Sec 4.3 acknowledges inconsistency vs. evaluator-error conflation but does not resolve it empirically.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds/runs are reported for the trend curves and Tables 1-2; given LLM stochasticity and long-horizon dynamics, some reported differences (e.g., a few points in Table 2) may not be statistically reliable.

Hyperparameters for deletion strategies (periods, thresholds beta, retrieval-frequency cutoffs) are set ad hoc and vary per agent, raising the question of whether conclusions are sensitive to these choices; no sensitivity analysis is provided.

The human (strict) evaluator is simulated via ground-truth comparison rather than actual human judgment, and only one backbone is used for the main table; both choices are acknowledged but weaken external validity.

The contribution is purely empirical with no theoretical grounding or formal characterization (acknowledged in Limitations); findings such as 'noisy additions can hurt' and 'quality-filtered memory helps' are plausible and, in part, expected, which tempers the novelty of the central results.

strengths: Systematic and well-scoped empirical study of two fundamental memory operations (addition and deletion) across four agents spanning synthetic and real task domains (EHR, autonomous driving, IoT traffic), which strengthens the generalizability of the observations

The controlled synthetic RegAgent environment is a sensible methodological choice, enabling direct measurement of error and clean isolation of the experience-following phenomenon (near-perfect input-output similarity correlation)

The identified phenomena—experience-following, error propagation, and misaligned experience replay—are clearly defined, and the error-free retrieval ablation (Figures 4, 13) provides a plausible mechanistic explanation for the observed long-term dynamics
The history-based deletion strategy grounded in downstream utility is a simple, practical contribution, and the resource-constraint and distribution-shift experiments add ecological relevance
Code, prompts, hyperparameters, and multiple LLM backbones (GPT-4o/4o-mini, 4.1-mini, DeepSeek-V3) are documented in extensive appendices, supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: The central findings are largely expected: noisy/unfiltered memory hurts long-term performance, and a stronger quality filter helps. The key conclusion—'use a reliable evaluator'—borders on tautological, since the best-performing 'strict' evaluator is essentially an oracle with ground-truth access, which is unavailable in the practical settings the paper motivates

Evidence that the conclusions generalize is limited: the main experiments use a single backbone (GPT-4o-mini), additional backbones appear only in appendices under reduced configurations, and no statistical significance testing, error bars, or repeated runs are reported for the headline Table 1/Table 2 results

The 'misaligned experience replay' analysis is indirect; the paper conflates evaluator-induced error with context misalignment and does not disentangle them, so the framing of three distinct phenomena overstates what the evidence supports

Scope is restricted to retrieve-as-demonstration episodic memory with add/delete; more prevalent mechanisms (summarization, merging, reflection, structured updates) are excluded, so 'practical guidance for designing memory components' may not transfer to modern memory systems

Hyperparameters (similarity thresholds, deletion periods, utility thresholds, retrieval counts) vary per agent and their sensitivity is not ablated, raising questions about robustness of specific quantitative results
Figures 2, 5, and several appendix plots are difficult to read (small text, many overlapping series), and some trends discussed in the text are only weakly visible in them

Related work positioning is somewhat generous to itself: the observation that bad demonstrations degrade in-context learning is well documented, and the incremental novelty over such prior findings should be more carefully delineated

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant question—how Bearer [REDACTED] addition/deletion operations shape long-term LLM agent behavior—and frames it cleanly around two fundamental operations that are common across many agent frameworks, giving the study good generality.

The experimental design is well-conceived: a controllable synthetic agent (RegAgent) allows direct measurement of stored-memory noise and error, complemented by three real agents (EHRAgent, AgentDriver, CIC-IoT) spanning diverse tasks, input/output formats, and retrieval mechanisms, which strengthens the external validity of the findings.

The identified phenomena—experience-following, error propagation, and misaligned experience replay—are clearly defined, quantitatively characterized (e.g., input–output similarity correlations in Figure 3/9/12), and validated through controlled interventions such as the error-free (ground-truth substitution) variants, which go beyond mere correlation and support causal claims about memory quality.

The deletion study is constructive rather than purely diagnostic: the proposed history-based deletion with a utility evaluator is simple, well-motivated, and shown to improve both performance and memory footprint, including under distribution shift and fixed memory-capacity constraints—settings that increase practical relevance.

The paper is thorough in its appendices (agent details, prompts, hyperparameters, additional backbones including GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3, deleted-vs-retained record analyses), and the authors commit to releasing code and data, supporting reproducibility.

The finding that a fine-tuned evaluator trained on only 300 trajectories (C3) outperforms vanilla LLM judges and even approaches oracle (strict) filtering is a useful, actionable insight for practitioners building memory modules.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor is limited: results appear to come from single runs without repeated seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite visibly noisy running curves (e.g., Figures 2, 7, 8). Several reported gaps (e.g., some deletion effects) are modest relative to this variance, which weakens confidence in some claims.

The main results (Table 1, Table 2) rely almost entirely on GPT-4o-mini as the backbone; the stronger backbones appear only for AgentDriver in the appendix. The generalizability of the central conclusions across models is therefore not fully established.

Several findings largely confirm intuitive expectations—noisy memory degrades performance, strict selection helps, evaluator quality matters—so the conceptual novelty is moderate. The 'experience-following' property is closely related to well-known demonstration-imitation behavior in in-context learning and prior work on experiential agents (e.g., ExpeL), and the paper could better delineate what is genuinely new beyond the memory-bank setting.

The 'strict' (human/oracle) addition baseline uses ground-truth matching, which is impractical in most real deployments; while the fine-tuned C3 evaluator partially mitigates this, the headline 'strict' results may overstate the achievable benefit in realistic settings.

There is no comparison against existing memory-management systems or more sophisticated baselines from the cited literature (e.g., MemoryBank-style forgetting, A-mem, structural transformation or reflection mechanisms), so the positioning relative to prior practical methods is incomplete; the study is restricted to plain addition/deletion as acknowledged in the Limitations.

Hyperparameters for deletion strategies (period, alpha, beta, retrieval-frequency thresholds) differ per agent and their sensitivity is not systematically analyzed, making it hard to assess robustness of the deletion conclusions to tuning choices.

The 'misaligned experience replay' explanation is only indirectly supported (via KDE of record errors in Figure 6); the hypothesized inconsistency/misalignment factor is not directly measured, leaving this part of the analysis somewhat speculative.
